organization.name: The Church of Orra
organization.entry:
The Church of Orra

Orra is the obscure sailor’s goddess of safe passage, returning travelers, and the small lights that keep the lost from becoming permanently lost. The Church of Orra was the first religion established on the isle. It is not Fogport’s largest faith, nor its wealthiest, nor its most politically useful. It survives because sailors, lamplighters, tram conductors, searchers, dock families, and people who have waited too long at a window still need somewhere to bring a lamp.

The Goddess and Her First Saint

Orra is not a queen, a war goddess, or a patron of conquest. She is usually represented as a veiled woman carrying a lamp in one hand and a length of rope in the other. Her priests teach that a safe return is not guaranteed; it is something made possible by attention, memory, and someone keeping a light alive.

Saint Orra was once an unnamed woman priestess serving Orra at the little lighthouse chapel of the isle. During the Black Founding Storm, 372 years ago, she climbed the chapel tower and burned its pews, books, doors, and roof to keep one harbor light alive for three nights. More than a hundred boats followed it home. At dawn she was gone. Scorched footprints went up the tower, but none came down.

The Church teaches that Orra guided the light, while the priestess chose to become its keeper. The woman was named Saint Orra afterward: Orra’s first saint, and a reminder that devotion is often an act of maintenance rather than spectacle.

Oldest Faith, Smallest Voice

The island was discovered 838 years ago. A small chapel to Orra followed soon after, and the settlement around it grew into Fogfort. The Black Founding Storm came later, bringing Fogport’s first green fog, which never left. As the town became a trade hub, its iron piers expanded for roughly a century and the island’s newer institutions, royal household, guilds, and imported religions eclipsed Orra’s chapel network.

The Church never truly centralized. Its chapels are tide-marked rooms, lamp closets, shrine alcoves, and small sanctuaries tucked into stations and harbor buildings. A chapel may have a priest, a lamplighter, a retired navigator, or simply the person who has kept its key longest. The church’s old claim is not that it owns Fogport, but that it remembers who is still outside it.

Saint Orra’s Colossus

The most visible Orrian monument is Saint Orra’s Colossus, the colossal bronze woman raised by House Heliot and surrounded by Grand Heliot Station. One hand reaches outward; the other carries the vast caged lantern called the Last Light. Her face is sealed beneath an unbroken bronze cowl. The station was meant to make Orra legible as a royal symbol. The church quietly rejects that interpretation.

At the plinth, pilgrims leave blue thread, keys, tram tickets, sailors’ knots, children’s shoes, and tiny unlit lamps. The inscription reads: ORRA BELONGS TO THOSE STILL OUTSIDE. At night, the raised lantern can be seen above the fog. It has not been officially lit since the Catastrophe, but Fogporters insist it sometimes burns when someone desperately needs to find the way home.

Keepers and Practices

Orrian clergy are variously called Keepers of the Light, Bluehands, lantern priests, chapel tenders, or simply auntie, uncle, navigator, or keeper. Their authority comes from tending things: lamps, names, ropes, tide charts, lost-property shelves, and the stories of those who failed to return.

The Leaving Light

Before a ship departs, the crew lights a small blue lamp at the harbor chapel. The lamp remains burning after the ship disappears into the fog, tended by the ship’s family, the chapel keeper, or a lamplighter.

It is extinguished only when the ship returns.

If the flame goes out while the ship is still away, someone relights it—but not before recording the ship’s name in the chapel’s Book of Unreturned Lights.

Other Rites

  • The Knot of Return: A sailor ties a knot for every person expected home. The final knot is left loose until the voyage ends.
  • The Bluehand: A departing traveler presses a blue-stained thumbprint into the chapel ledger. The mark is washed away only when they return.
  • The Empty Berth: When a body cannot be recovered, the church keeps an empty place at the harbor table and speaks the dead person’s name during the Sea Funeral.
  • The Three Questions: A lost person is asked where they came from, what they were following, and who might be waiting. The answers are written down before directions are offered.
  • The Last Light: On the Long Night of Lanterns, Orrians carry unlit lamps through the fog and light them only at another keeper’s flame.

Public Reputation

Fogport’s respectable powers find the Church harmless when it is blessing a tram crew, recording a missing child, or keeping lamps lit during a blackout. They find it irritating when its keepers insist that a person has not been “lost” merely because the Civic Order has stopped looking. The church has little money, few grand offices, and no appetite for public conversion. Its influence is practical and stubborn: a door opened after curfew, a name preserved, a boat guided home, a child recognized at the wrong end of the city.

It is not aligned with the Divided Saint. The cult’s storm sermons and claims about a deeper power are considered a dangerous blasphemy against Orra’s central lesson: the storm is not the destination, and no light is made holier by swallowing the people who follow it.

Rumors and Likelihoods

  • Likely: Some old chapels keep duplicate ledgers because the first copy is believed to become unreliable after a death at sea.
  • Likely: The lamplighters know routes through the fog that do not appear on any civic map.
  • Possible: The Last Light shines for genuinely lost people, but another person somewhere in Fogport becomes lost instead.
  • Possible: The sealed stair beneath Saint Orra’s Colossus reaches old tram tunnels and a buried royal complex.
  • Unproven: The Colossus sometimes turns its head toward the person who needs it most.
  • Unproven: Orra’s church has a hidden signal for ships that should not be allowed to return.
  • False, or dangerously incomplete: The Church of Orra wants to restore the Black Founding Storm. That is the Divided Saint’s interpretation, not the church’s.

gm_post.name: GAMEMASTER SECRETS — The Church of Orra
gm_post.entry:
GM Secrets: The Church of Orra

The public article is broadly true, but the church has spent centuries mistaking endurance for safety. Its oldest records are not a clean theology; they are maintenance logs, names, weather marks, and desperate annotations written by people who saw things in the green fog and chose to keep the lamps burning anyway.

What the Church Does Not Know

The Last Light was incorporated into the Continuance Engine during House Heliot’s great civic works. The sealed stair under Saint Orra’s Colossus leads toward tram tunnels and a buried royal complex. During the Catastrophe, the lantern burned black for thirteen days. When the statues turned inward, Saint Orra’s head bowed toward the Old Palace.

The church is correct that the Divided Saint is wrong about Saint Orra. It is not correct that the storm is harmless. The storm may be a wound, a door, or a weather system with a memory. The Divided Saint’s reaching hand belongs to an ancient revenant or lich-like intelligence called the Unreturned, buried beneath Fogfort. The church has no reliable name for it, but some of its oldest ledgers contain the same symbol: a lamp drawn with its flame pointing downward.

Byl Hasbaine

Byl’s wild magic produces the kind of accidental wrongness Orrian keepers fear most: a road that remains after the street is gone, a name that belongs to two people, a door that opens onto the memory of a harbor. Some young Bluehands think he may be a “storm child,” chosen by the same force that once carried the boats home. Older keepers see him as a dangerous moving landmark.

A chapel may ask Byl to help find someone who has vanished into the city, but the request is not innocent. The church wants to know whether his magic can locate the missing without making someone else disappear. If Byl learns what the Last Light takes in exchange for its guidance, he may decide the church has been preserving a bargain rather than a blessing.

Lott

Lott is treated by some keepers as a sailor who has returned from a voyage nobody can document. His presence unsettles the empty-berth rite: a few lamps lean toward him, and the Book of Unreturned Lights contains names written in handwriting disturbingly similar to his.

A senior keeper may ask Lott to carry an empty coffin in the Sea Funeral. The coffin is not meant for him. It is a test, a lure, and possibly a container for something that has been waiting beneath the tide chapel. If Lott refuses, the church may still record his name as “returned.” If he accepts, something in the fog may recognize him as crew.

Conflict with Byl and Lott

  • A chapel keeper asks Byl to find a missing child; Byl discovers that the child is safe, but the child’s “original” name is trapped in a lamp beneath the Colossus.
  • Lott’s reflection appears in the black glass of the Last Light, wearing a different face and holding a key to the sealed stair.
  • The Church asks both of them to investigate a Book of Unreturned Lights whose newest entry is dated tomorrow.
  • The Divided Saint tries to recruit them by claiming the Church of Orra has always known the storm is alive.
  • A keeper tells the truth: the church can guide a lost person home, but it cannot promise that home will still recognize them.
